title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
section: The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
text:
The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem






Note



In this section, connect the A/B test to a formal statistical framework. Address each of the following ideas:

Each visitor either signs up or does not, so we can model each visitor’s outcome as a draw from a Bernoulli distribution with parameter \(\pi\), the probability of signing up.
Because the CTA a visitor sees may influence their probability of signing up, we allow the parameter to differ across groups: visitors who see CTA A have sign-up probability \(\pi_A\), and visitors who see CTA B have sign-up probability \(\pi_B\). Each visitor can either sign up (1) or not (0).
The quantity we care about is \(\theta = \pi_A - \pi_B\), the difference in sign-up rates between the two CTAs.
Our estimator of \(\theta\) is the difference in sample means, \(\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\). (Since each observation is either 0 or 1, the sample mean is simply the proportion of visitors who signed up — so \(\bar{X}_A = \hat\pi_A\) and \(\bar{X}_B = \hat\pi_B\).)

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Simulating Data






Note




Write a brief paragraph for the reader explaining that in the real world we would not know the true values of \(\pi_A\) and \(\pi_B\), but for the purpose of this exercise we will set them ourselves so that we can study the behavior of our estimator when we know the truth.
Suppose \(\pi_A = 0.22\) and \(\pi_B = 0.18\), so the true difference is \(\theta = 0.04\).
Using a language of your choice, simulate 1,000 draws from each of the two Bernoulli distributions (2,000 total). Store the results so you can use them in the sections that follow.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Law of Large Numbers






Note




Write an introductory sentence or two explaining the Law of Large Numbers to the reader: as the sample size grows, the sample mean converges to the population mean. Connect this back to our estimator — the LLN is what gives us confidence that \(\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\) will be close to the true \(\theta\) when our sample is large enough.
Then demonstrate this visually. Using the simulated data from the previous section, compute the element-wise differences between the CTA A draws and the CTA B draws to get a vector of 1,000 differences. Calculate the cumulative average of that vector (i.e., the running mean after 1 draw, after 2 draws, …, after 1,000 draws) and plot it against the number of observations.
The plot should show a noisy average when only a few observations are included that settles down and converges toward the true difference of 0.04 as the sample size grows.
After the plot, write a few sentences explaining what the reader should take away from it.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Bootstrap Standard Errors






Note




Now that we “trust” our estimator, the next natural question is: how precise is it? We would like to report not just a point estimate of \(\theta\) but also a confidence interval that communicates our uncertainty.
Write a short introduction explaining the idea of bootstrapping to the reader. The bootstrap is a resampling method that lets us estimate the variability of a statistic without relying on a closed-form formula. We resample (with replacement) from our observed data many times, compute the statistic of interest on each resample, and use the standard deviation of those resampled statistics as our estimate of the standard error.
Then carry out the following steps:

From your 1,000 CTA A draws and 1,000 CTA B draws, draw a bootstrap resample of size 1,000 (with replacement) from each group. Compute \(\hat\theta^* = \bar{X}_A^* - \bar{X}_B^*\) for that resample.
Repeat step 1 a total of 1,000 times to produce a vector of 1,000 bootstrapped estimates of \(\theta\).
Compute the standard deviation of those 1,000 values. This is your bootstrapped standard error.
Compare it to the analytical standard error. For the difference in means of two independent Bernoulli samples, the standard error formula is:


\[
SE(\hat\theta) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat\pi_A(1 - \hat\pi_A)}{n_A} + \frac{\hat\pi_B(1 - \hat\pi_B)}{n_B}}
\]
where \(\hat\pi_A\) and \(\hat\pi_B\) are the sample proportions and \(n_A\) and \(n_B\) are the sample sizes.

Report both the bootstrapped standard error and the analytical standard error and comment on how close they are to each other. Then use the bootstrapped standard error to construct a 95% confidence interval for \(\theta\) and interpret it for the reader.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Central Limit Theorem






Note




Write a short introduction explaining the Central Limit Theorem to the reader: regardless of the shape of the underlying population distribution, the sampling distribution of the sample mean (and therefore of the difference in sample means) becomes approximately Normal as the sample size grows.
Then demonstrate this visually by creating four histograms, one for each of the following sample sizes: \(n \in \{25, 50, 100, 500\}\).
For each sample size \(n\):

Draw \(n\) observations from the CTA A distribution and \(n\) observations from the CTA B distribution.
Compute \(\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\).
Repeat steps 1–2 a total of 1,000 times to produce 1,000 values of \(\hat\theta\).
Plot a histogram of those 1,000 values.

Arrange the four histograms so they can be compared easily (e.g., in a 2x2 grid with consistent x-axis scales).
After the plots, write a few sentences explaining what the reader should observe: at small sample sizes the histogram may look rough or asymmetric, but as \(n\) increases the distribution of \(\hat\theta\) becomes smoother and more bell-shaped, illustrating the Central Limit Theorem in action.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Hypothesis Testing






Note




Now that we have seen the CLT in action — that the sampling distribution of \(\hat\theta\) is approximately Normal for large samples — we can use this result to perform a formal hypothesis test.
Write a paragraph explaining what a hypothesis test is to the reader. We set up a null hypothesis \(H_0: \theta = 0\) (i.e., the two CTAs produce the same sign-up rate) and an alternative hypothesis \(H_1: \theta \neq 0\). The goal is to assess whether the data provide enough evidence to reject \(H_0\).
Then explain why we standardize \(\hat\theta\) to form a test statistic. We compute:

\[
z = \frac{\hat\theta - 0}{SE(\hat\theta)}
\]

Walk the reader through the logic of this standardization step by step:

By the CLT, we know that \(\hat\theta\) is approximately Normal for large samples. Under \(H_0\), the mean of that distribution is 0.
When we divide a Normal random variable by its standard deviation, we get a standard Normal \(N(0,1)\). So under \(H_0\), \(z \;\dot\sim\; N(0,1)\).
This means we know the distribution of our test statistic under the null, which is exactly what we need to compute a p-value.

Explain to the reader why this is sometimes called a “t-test” even though the test statistic follows an approximate Normal distribution, not a t-distribution. The classical t-test arises when the data are drawn from a Normal distribution and the variance must be estimated — the ratio then follows an exact t-distribution. In our setting the data are Bernoulli (not Normal), so there is no exact t-distribution result. The CLT gives us approximate Normality, and since we estimate the SE from the data, what we are really doing is closer to a z-test. In practice, for large samples the t-distribution and the standard Normal are nearly identical, so the distinction has little practical consequence — but it is important to understand why.
Using your simulated data, compute the test statistic and its associated p-value (using the standard Normal distribution as the reference). Interpret the result for the reader.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The T-Test as a Regression






Note




It turns out that the two-sample test we just ran is mathematically equivalent to a simple linear regression. Understanding this connection is useful because it means the same machinery — and the same software — that you use for regression can also perform hypothesis tests, and it generalizes naturally to more complex experimental designs.
Explain the setup to the reader. Stack the CTA A and CTA B data into a single dataset with two columns: an outcome \(Y_i\) (1 if the visitor signed up, 0 otherwise) and an indicator \(D_i\) (1 if the visitor saw CTA A, 0 if they saw CTA B). Then fit the regression:

\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \varepsilon_i
\]

Walk through the interpretation of the coefficients:

\(\beta_0\) is the expected value of \(Y_i\) when \(D_i = 0\) — i.e., the mean of the B group, which estimates \(\pi_B\).
\(\beta_0 + \beta_1\) is the expected value of \(Y_i\) when \(D_i = 1\) — i.e., the mean of the A group, which estimates \(\pi_A\).
Therefore \(\beta_1 = \pi_A - \pi_B = \theta\), and the OLS estimate \(\hat\beta_1\) is numerically identical to \(\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\).

Fit this regression using your simulated data. Report the coefficient estimate \(\hat\beta_1\), its standard error, its t-statistic, and its p-value. Compare these to the values you computed in the previous section using the two-sample approach — they should match (up to a small difference in how the standard error is computed; standard OLS assumes a single pooled variance, while the two-sample formula we used assumes separate variances for each group).
Explain to the reader why this equivalence matters: the regression framework makes it easy to add controls, interactions, or additional treatment arms, all while producing the same inference in the simple case.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Problem with Peeking






Note




Your boss is impatient. Rather than waiting until all 1,000 visitors have been assigned to each group, she wants to run the hypothesis test after every 100 visitors per group — peeking at the results after 100, 200, 300, …, up to 1,000 visitors per group (10 tests in total). If any of those tests comes back significant at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) level, she wants to declare a winner and stop the experiment early.
Explain to the reader why this is problematic under classical frequentist statistics. The key issue is that a single test at \(\alpha = 0.05\) has a 5% chance of a false positive (rejecting \(H_0\) when it is actually true). But when you conduct multiple tests on accumulating data, each peek is another opportunity to get a false positive. The overall probability of at least one false rejection across all the peeks is much higher than 5%.
Demonstrate this with a simulation. The idea is as follows:

Set up a world where the null hypothesis is true: \(\pi_A = \pi_B = 0.20\) (i.e., \(\theta = 0\), there is no difference between the CTAs).
Simulate a single experiment: draw 1,000 observations for group A and 1,000 for group B. After every 100 observations per group (at \(n = 100, 200, \ldots, 1000\)), compute the z-statistic and p-value. Record whether any of the 10 p-values falls below 0.05.
Repeat step 2 a total of 10,000 times to simulate 10,000 experiments.
Compute the fraction of those 10,000 experiments in which at least one peek produced a significant result. This is the empirical false positive rate under peeking.

Compare this to the nominal 5% false positive rate of a single test. Report the result and explain to the reader why peeking inflates the Type I error rate and what this means in practice for running A/B tests.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Running a website comes with a constant stream of small decisions: what font to use, where to put the navigation menu, and — perhaps most importantly — how to phrase the moments when you ask visitors to take action. On my website’s landing page, visitors can sign up for a newsletter. The question I want to answer is deceptively simple: does the exact wording of that invitation matter?
To find out, I designed an A/B test. Half of the visitors landing on my page are randomly shown CTA A — “Sign up for our newsletter here!” — and the other half see CTA B — “Stay up to date by signing up!” I then compare the sign-up rates between the two groups.
The beauty of random assignment is that it makes the two groups statistically equivalent in every way except the CTA they see. Any difference in sign-up rates can therefore be attributed to the wording itself, not to pre-existing differences between the visitors. Rather than just running the test and reporting the outcome, this post uses the A/B test as a vehicle for exploring the core ideas that underpin classical frequentist statistics: the Law of Large Numbers, the bootstrap, the Central Limit Theorem, hypothesis testing, and the regression connection — all illustrated through simulation.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
section: The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
text:
The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
Each visitor who lands on the page either signs up or doesn’t. That binary outcome is naturally modeled as a draw from a Bernoulli distribution with some probability parameter \(\pi\). Because the CTA a visitor sees may influence their decision, we allow the parameter to differ across groups: visitors who see CTA A have sign-up probability \(\pi_A\), and visitors who see CTA B have sign-up probability \(\pi_B\).
The quantity we ultimately care about is:
\[\theta = \pi_A - \pi_B\]
the difference in sign-up rates. If \(\theta > 0\), CTA A is better; if \(\theta < 0\), CTA B is better; if \(\theta \approx 0\), it doesn’t much matter.
We don’t know \(\theta\) — we have to estimate it from data. Our estimator is the difference in sample proportions:
\[\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B = \hat\pi_A - \hat\pi_B\]
Because each observation is either 0 or 1, the sample mean is exactly the fraction of visitors who signed up, making this estimator both intuitive and easy to compute. The rest of this post is about understanding how reliable this estimator is.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Simulating Data
In a real experiment we would not know the true values of \(\pi_A\) and \(\pi_B\) — that is precisely what we are trying to learn. But for this exercise we will set them ourselves so that we can study how our estimator behaves when we know the ground truth.
Let’s suppose \(\pi_A = 0.22\) and \(\pi_B = 0.18\), so the true difference is \(\theta = 0.04\). CTA A is four percentage points better — a meaningful but not enormous lift. We simulate 1,000 visitors in each group.

pi_A = 0.22
pi_B = 0.18
n    = 1000

group_A = rng.binomial(1, pi_A, n)
group_B = rng.binomial(1, pi_B, n)

theta_true = pi_A - pi_B
theta_hat  = group_A.mean() - group_B.mean()

print(f"True difference:      {theta_true:.4f}")
print(f"Estimated difference: {theta_hat:.4f}")

True difference:      0.0400
Estimated difference: 0.0250


Our point estimate is already in the right neighborhood. But how confident should we be in that number? The sections below answer that question systematically.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Law of Large Numbers
The Law of Large Numbers (LLN) tells us that as the sample size grows, the sample mean converges to the true population mean. Applied here: as we accumulate more visitors, \(\hat\pi_A \to \pi_A\) and \(\hat\pi_B \to \pi_B\), which means \(\hat\theta \to \theta\). This is the foundational guarantee that our estimator will eventually get it right — if we collect enough data.
We can visualize the LLN directly. For each visitor \(k = 1, 2, \ldots, 1{,}000\), we compute the difference between the \(k\)-th CTA A outcome and the \(k\)-th CTA B outcome, then track the cumulative average of those differences as we add one observation at a time.

diffs   = group_A - group_B
cum_avg = np.cumsum(diffs) / np.arange(1, n + 1)









Figure 1: Cumulative average of the per-visitor differences between CTA A and CTA B outcomes. The dashed line marks the true θ = 0.04.





The plot makes the LLN tangible. With only a handful of observations the running average bounces around wildly — a single sign-up swings the estimate dramatically when the denominator is small. But as we accumulate visitors the noise averages out, and the estimate settles steadily toward the true \(\theta = 0.04\). By the time we have 500 or more visitors per group, the estimate is reliably close to the truth.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Bootstrap Standard Errors
Knowing that our estimator converges to the truth is reassuring, but it doesn’t tell us how precise it is for any specific sample size. We want not just a point estimate \(\hat\theta\) but also a confidence interval that honestly communicates our uncertainty.
One elegant way to estimate the variability of any statistic is the bootstrap. Instead of deriving a formula for the standard error from first principles, we let the data speak for themselves. The idea:

Treat your observed sample as if it were the population.
Draw a new sample of the same size with replacement from it.
Compute \(\hat\theta^*\) on this “resample.”
Repeat many times and look at the spread of the resulting \(\hat\theta^*\) values.

The standard deviation of the bootstrapped estimates is our bootstrapped standard error — a data-driven measure of how much \(\hat\theta\) would vary across different samples of the same size.

B = 1000
boot_ests = np.empty(B)

for b in range(B):
    resamp_A    = rng.choice(group_A, size=n, replace=True)
    resamp_B    = rng.choice(group_B, size=n, replace=True)
    boot_ests[b] = resamp_A.mean() - resamp_B.mean()

se_boot = boot_ests.std(ddof=1)

pi_hat_A      = group_A.mean()
pi_hat_B      = group_B.mean()
se_analytical = np.sqrt(
    pi_hat_A * (1 - pi_hat_A) / n +
    pi_hat_B * (1 - pi_hat_B) / n
)

ci_lower = theta_hat - 1.96 * se_boot
ci_upper = theta_hat + 1.96 * se_boot

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Central Limit Theorem
The bootstrap gave us a practical way to measure uncertainty. But there is a deeper theoretical result at work: the Central Limit Theorem (CLT).
The CLT states that regardless of the shape of the underlying population distribution, the sampling distribution of the sample mean becomes approximately Normal as the sample size grows. Because \(\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\) is a difference of two sample means, the same result applies: for large enough samples, the distribution of \(\hat\theta\) across repeated experiments is approximately Normal, even though the underlying data are Bernoulli (just zeros and ones).
To see this in action, we run a simulation for four different sample sizes — \(n \in \{25, 50, 100, 500\}\). For each, we repeat the experiment 1,000 times and plot the distribution of \(\hat\theta\).

sample_sizes = [25, 50, 100, 500]
n_reps       = 1000

clt_results = {}
for n_sim in sample_sizes:
    theta_hats = np.array([
        rng.binomial(1, pi_A, n_sim).mean() - rng.binomial(1, pi_B, n_sim).mean()
        for _ in range(n_reps)
    ])
    clt_results[n_sim] = theta_hats









Figure 2: Sampling distribution of θ̂ for four sample sizes, each based on 1,000 simulated experiments. The red dashed line marks the true θ = 0.04.





At \(n = 25\) the histogram is lumpy and asymmetric — there simply aren’t enough observations for the averaging to kick in. As we move to \(n = 50\) and \(n = 100\), the bell shape becomes increasingly apparent. By \(n = 500\) the distribution is strikingly Normal and tightly centered on the true \(\theta = 0.04\). This progression is the CLT in action, and it’s the theoretical backbone for everything in the next section.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Hypothesis Testing
Now that we’ve confirmed (visually and theoretically) that the sampling distribution of \(\hat\theta\) is approximately Normal for large samples, we can use that fact to conduct a formal hypothesis test.
We frame the question as a choice between two competing claims:

Null hypothesis \(H_0\): \(\theta = 0\) — the two CTAs perform identically.
Alternative hypothesis \(H_1\): \(\theta \neq 0\) — one CTA is better than the other.


The Test Statistic
To assess whether our estimate is surprising under \(H_0\), we form the z-statistic:
\[z = \frac{\hat\theta - 0}{SE(\hat\theta)}\]
The logic step by step:

By the CLT, \(\hat\theta\) is approximately Normal for large samples. Under \(H_0\), the mean of that distribution is 0.
Dividing a Normal random variable by its standard deviation gives a standard Normal \(N(0,1)\). So under \(H_0\), \(z \;\dot\sim\; N(0,1)\).
Because we know the null distribution of \(z\), we can ask: how probable is a value at least as extreme as what we observed? That probability is the p-value.



Why Is It Sometimes Called a “t-test”?
When textbooks call this a t-test, they invoke a result from a different setting: if the raw data are Normally distributed and the variance is unknown, the standardized statistic follows an exact \(t\)-distribution. In our case the data are Bernoulli, so there’s no exact \(t\)-distribution result. The CLT gives us approximate Normality, making this more precisely a z-test. For large samples the \(t\) and \(N(0,1)\) are nearly identical, so the distinction rarely matters in practice — but it’s important to understand why.

z_stat  = theta_hat / se_analytical
p_value = 2 * stats.norm.sf(abs(z_stat))

print(f"θ̂       = {theta_hat:.4f}")
print(f"SE      = {se_analytical:.4f}")
print(f"z-stat  = {z_stat:.4f}")
print(f"p-value = {p_value:.4f}")

SE      = 0.0183

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The T-Test as a Regression
Here is something surprising: the two-sample test we just ran is mathematically identical to a simple linear regression. This connection is more than a curiosity — it shows that the OLS machinery subsumes hypothesis testing as a special case, and it points toward how to generalize beyond two groups.

The Setup
We stack the CTA A and CTA B data into a single dataset with two columns:

\(Y_i\): 1 if visitor \(i\) signed up, 0 otherwise
\(D_i\): 1 if visitor \(i\) saw CTA A, 0 if they saw CTA B

Then we fit:
\[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \varepsilon_i\]


Interpreting the Coefficients

\(\beta_0\) is the expected value of \(Y_i\) when \(D_i = 0\) — the mean of the B group, which estimates \(\pi_B\).
\(\beta_0 + \beta_1\) is the expected value when \(D_i = 1\) — the mean of the A group, which estimates \(\pi_A\).
Therefore \(\beta_1 = \pi_A - \pi_B = \theta\), and OLS produces \(\hat\beta_1 = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\).


import statsmodels.api as sm

Y = np.concatenate([group_A, group_B])
D = np.concatenate([np.ones(n), np.zeros(n)])
X = sm.add_constant(D)

model   = sm.OLS(Y, X).fit()
b1      = model.params[1]
se_b1   = model.bse[1]
t_stat  = model.tvalues[1]
p_reg   = model.pvalues[1]

The standard errors differ very slightly because OLS assumes a single pooled variance, while our two-sample formula uses separate estimates for each group — a distinction that matters little when sample sizes are equal and proportions are similar.
The deeper point: once you express a comparison as a regression, you can add covariates to reduce noise, include multiple treatment arms, or model interactions between the treatment and visitor characteristics — all using the same software and the same interpretation framework.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Problem with Peeking
Our analysis so far has been clean: collect 1,000 observations per group, then run one test. But in practice, data arrives sequentially and the temptation to peek at interim results is real. Your boss wants to know if there’s a winner after every 100 new visitors. If any peek shows significance at \(\alpha = 0.05\), she wants to stop the experiment and declare victory.
This seems harmless — after all, each individual test uses the same \(\alpha = 0.05\) threshold. But it isn’t harmless, and the simulation below shows exactly why.

The Problem
Each test at \(\alpha = 0.05\) has a 5% chance of a false positive when \(H_0\) is true. But 10 peeks mean 10 chances to get lucky. The probability that at least one of those tests produces a false significant result is far higher than 5%.


Simulation
We set up a world where \(H_0\) is true (\(\pi_A = \pi_B = 0.20\), so \(\theta = 0\)) and simulate 10,000 experiments. In each experiment we peek after every 100 visitors per group.

n_sims   = 10_000
peek_at  = np.arange(100, 1001, 100)
pi_null  = 0.20

false_positives = 0

for _ in range(n_sims):
    A = rng.binomial(1, pi_null, 1000)
    B = rng.binomial(1, pi_null, 1000)

    for k in peek_at:
        pa = A[:k].mean()
        pb = B[:k].mean()
        se_k = np.sqrt(pa * (1 - pa) / k + pb * (1 - pb) / k)
        if se_k == 0:
            continue
        z_k = (pa - pb) / se_k
        p_k = 2 * stats.norm.sf(abs(z_k))
        if p_k < 0.05:
            false_positives += 1
            break

fp_rate = false_positives / n_sims
print(f"Empirical false positive rate with peeking: {fp_rate:.1%}")
print(f"Nominal false positive rate (single test): 5.0%")

Empirical false positive rate with peeking: 19.4%
Nominal false positive rate (single test): 5.0%










Figure 3: Empirical false positive rate under a peeking strategy (10 checkpoints) versus a pre-specified single test at α = 0.05.





The empirical false positive rate under peeking is approximately 19.4% — roughly 3.9× the nominal 5%. In other words, even when the two CTAs are identical, the peeking strategy would declare a winner in about 19% of experiments. You would routinely ship a change that has no real effect, simply because you looked at the data too many times.
This is not a minor technicality. It is one of the most common pitfalls in applied A/B testing. The frequentist guarantee — “if \(H_0\) is true, I will wrongly reject it only 5% of the time” — applies to a pre-specified single test, not to a repeated-peeking strategy. If you want to peek, you need methods designed for sequential testing (such as sequential probability ratio tests or alpha-spending functions) that control the false positive rate across all peeks jointly.

All simulations in this post were run in Python with a fixed random seed for reproducibility.

title: Replication of Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
Does raising the minimum wage destroy jobs? The conventional economic prediction is yes: a higher wage floor prices low-skill workers out of the labor market. Card and Krueger (1994) challenged this view by exploiting a natural experiment that New Jersey handed them in April 1992, when the state raised its minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.05 per hour while neighboring Pennsylvania left its wage floor unchanged.
The authors surveyed 410 fast-food restaurants (Burger King, KFC, Roy Rogers, and Wendy’s) in both states before the increase (February–March 1992) and after (November–December 1992). Because New Jersey and Pennsylvania share a border, labor markets, and business conditions, the two states serve as near-perfect treatment and control groups. Any difference in employment growth between NJ and PA that emerged after April 1992—but not before—can be attributed to the minimum wage increase rather than to unobserved economic trends.
This identification strategy is called difference-in-differences (DiD):
\[
\hat{\delta}_{\text{DiD}} = \underbrace{(\bar{E}^{NJ}_{\text{after}} - \bar{E}^{NJ}_{\text{before}})}_{\text{NJ change}} - \underbrace{(\bar{E}^{PA}_{\text{after}} - \bar{E^{PA}_{\text{before}}})}_{\text{PA change}}
\]
The DiD estimator removes two confounders at once: time-invariant store characteristics (like location quality) are eliminated by the within-state before–after difference, and common time trends (like macroeconomic conditions) are eliminated by the NJ-minus-PA comparison. The key identifying assumption—called parallel trends—is that in the absence of the NJ minimum wage increase, NJ and PA employment would have evolved similarly.

Difference-in-Differences: FTE Employment Before and After NJ Minimum Wage Increase




Why DiD enables a causal conclusion. A simple before-and-after comparison of NJ stores would confound the minimum wage with any other event that occurred between the two surveys (e.g., a regional recession). A simple NJ-vs-PA comparison would confound the wage increase with any permanent differences between the two states (e.g., New Jersey being more urban). Differencing twice—across time and across states—cancels both threats simultaneously, leaving only variation that is both state-specific and time-varying. Under the parallel-trends assumption, the only state-specific time-varying shock was the minimum wage increase itself, so the DiD estimate is causal.
Card and Krueger’s finding—that the minimum wage increase had no detectable negative effect on employment, and possibly a positive one—sparked decades of debate and fundamentally changed how economists model labor markets, motivating theories of monopsony and search frictions that can accommodate a zero or positive employment response to minimum wage increases.

The DiD estimator removes two confounders at once: time-invariant store characteristics (like location quality) are eliminated by the within-state before–after difference, and common time trends (like macroeconomic conditions) are eliminated by the NJ-minus-PA comparison. The key identifying assumption—called parallel trends—is that in the absence of the NJ minimum wage increase, NJ and PA employment would have evolved similarly.

title: Replication of Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
Does raising the minimum wage destroy jobs? The conventional economic prediction is yes: a higher wage floor prices low-skill workers out of the labor market. Card and Krueger (1994) challenged this view by exploiting a natural experiment that New Jersey handed them in April 1992, when the state raised its minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.05 per hour while neighboring Pennsylvania left its wage floor unchanged.
The authors surveyed 410 fast-food restaurants (Burger King, KFC, Roy Rogers, and Wendy’s) in both states before the increase (February–March 1992) and after (November–December 1992). Because New Jersey and Pennsylvania share a border, labor markets, and business conditions, the two states serve as near-perfect treatment and control groups. Any difference in employment growth between NJ and PA that emerged after April 1992—but not before—can be attributed to the minimum wage increase rather than to unobserved economic trends.
This identification strategy is called difference-in-differences (DiD):
\[
\hat{\delta}_{\text{DiD}} = \underbrace{(\bar{E}^{NJ}_{\text{after}} - \bar{E}^{NJ}_{\text{before}})}_{\text{NJ change}} - \underbrace{(\bar{E}^{PA}_{\text{after}} - \bar{E^{PA}_{\text{before}}})}_{\text{PA change}}
\]
The DiD estimator removes two confounders at once: time-invariant store characteristics (like location quality) are eliminated by the within-state before–after difference, and common time trends (like macroeconomic conditions) are eliminated by the NJ-minus-PA comparison. The key identifying assumption—called parallel trends—is that in the absence of the NJ minimum wage increase, NJ and PA employment would have evolved similarly.

Difference-in-Differences: FTE Employment Before and After NJ Minimum Wage Increase




Why DiD enables a causal conclusion. A simple before-and-after comparison of NJ stores would confound the minimum wage with any other event that occurred between the two surveys (e.g., a regional recession). A simple NJ-vs-PA comparison would confound the wage increase with any permanent differences between the two states (e.g., New Jersey being more urban). Differencing twice—across time and across states—cancels both threats simultaneously, leaving only variation that is both state-specific and time-varying. Under the parallel-trends assumption, the only state-specific time-varying shock was the minimum wage increase itself, so the DiD estimate is causal.
Card and Krueger’s finding—that the minimum wage increase had no detectable negative effect on employment, and possibly a positive one—sparked decades of debate and fundamentally changed how economists model labor markets, motivating theories of monopsony and search frictions that can accommodate a zero or positive employment response to minimum wage increases.

section: The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
text:
The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem






Note



In this section, connect the A/B test to a formal statistical framework. Address each of the following ideas:

Each visitor either signs up or does not, so we can model each visitor’s outcome as a draw from a Bernoulli distribution with parameter \(\pi\), the probability of signing up.
Because the CTA a visitor sees may influence their probability of signing up, we allow the parameter to differ across groups: visitors who see CTA A have sign-up probability \(\pi_A\), and visitors who see CTA B have sign-up probability \(\pi_B\). Each visitor can either sign up (1) or not (0).
The quantity we care about is \(\theta = \pi_A - \pi_B\), the difference in sign-up rates between the two CTAs.
Our estimator of \(\theta\) is the difference in sample means, \(\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\). (Since each observation is either 0 or 1, the sample mean is simply the proportion of visitors who signed up — so \(\bar{X}_A = \hat\pi_A\) and \(\bar{X}_B = \hat\pi_B\).)

Suppose \(\pi_A = 0.22\) and \(\pi_B = 0.18\), so the true difference is \(\theta = 0.04\).
Using a language of your choice, simulate 1,000 draws from each of the two Bernoulli distributions (2,000 total). Store the results so you can use them in the sections that follow.

The Law of Large Numbers






Note




Write an introductory sentence or two explaining the Law of Large Numbers to the reader: as the sample size grows, the sample mean converges to the population mean. Connect this back to our estimator — the LLN is what gives us confidence that \(\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\) will be close to the true \(\theta\) when our sample is large enough.
Then demonstrate this visually. Using the simulated data from the previous section, compute the element-wise differences between the CTA A draws and the CTA B draws to get a vector of 1,000 differences. Calculate the cumulative average of that vector (i.e., the running mean after 1 draw, after 2 draws, …, after 1,000 draws) and plot it against the number of observations.
The plot should show a noisy average when only a few observations are included that settles down and converges toward the true difference of 0.04 as the sample size grows.
After the plot, write a few sentences explaining what the reader should take away from it.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Bootstrap Standard Errors






Note




Now that we “trust” our estimator, the next natural question is: how precise is it? We would like to report not just a point estimate of \(\theta\) but also a confidence interval that communicates our uncertainty.
Write a short introduction explaining the idea of bootstrapping to the reader. The bootstrap is a resampling method that lets us estimate the variability of a statistic without relying on a closed-form formula. We resample (with replacement) from our observed data many times, compute the statistic of interest on each resample, and use the standard deviation of those resampled statistics as our estimate of the standard error.
Then carry out the following steps:

From your 1,000 CTA A draws and 1,000 CTA B draws, draw a bootstrap resample of size 1,000 (with replacement) from each group. Compute \(\hat\theta^* = \bar{X}_A^* - \bar{X}_B^*\) for that resample.
Repeat step 1 a total of 1,000 times to produce a vector of 1,000 bootstrapped estimates of \(\theta\).
Compute the standard deviation of those 1,000 values. This is your bootstrapped standard error.
Compare it to the analytical standard error. For the difference in means of two independent Bernoulli samples, the standard error formula is:


\[
SE(\hat\theta) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat\pi_A(1 - \hat\pi_A)}{n_A} + \frac{\hat\pi_B(1 - \hat\pi_B)}{n_B}}
\]
where \(\hat\pi_A\) and \(\hat\pi_B\) are the sample proportions and \(n_A\) and \(n_B\) are the sample sizes.

Report both the bootstrapped standard error and the analytical standard error and comment on how close they are to each other. Then use the bootstrapped standard error to construct a 95% confidence interval for \(\theta\) and interpret it for the reader.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Central Limit Theorem






Note




Write a short introduction explaining the Central Limit Theorem to the reader: regardless of the shape of the underlying population distribution, the sampling distribution of the sample mean (and therefore of the difference in sample means) becomes approximately Normal as the sample size grows.
Then demonstrate this visually by creating four histograms, one for each of the following sample sizes: \(n \in \{25, 50, 100, 500\}\).
For each sample size \(n\):

Draw \(n\) observations from the CTA A distribution and \(n\) observations from the CTA B distribution.
Compute \(\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\).
Repeat steps 1–2 a total of 1,000 times to produce 1,000 values of \(\hat\theta\).
Plot a histogram of those 1,000 values.

Arrange the four histograms so they can be compared easily (e.g., in a 2x2 grid with consistent x-axis scales).
After the plots, write a few sentences explaining what the reader should observe: at small sample sizes the histogram may look rough or asymmetric, but as \(n\) increases the distribution of \(\hat\theta\) becomes smoother and more bell-shaped, illustrating the Central Limit Theorem in action.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Hypothesis Testing






Note




Now that we have seen the CLT in action — that the sampling distribution of \(\hat\theta\) is approximately Normal for large samples — we can use this result to perform a formal hypothesis test.
Write a paragraph explaining what a hypothesis test is to the reader. We set up a null hypothesis \(H_0: \theta = 0\) (i.e., the two CTAs produce the same sign-up rate) and an alternative hypothesis \(H_1: \theta \neq 0\). The goal is to assess whether the data provide enough evidence to reject \(H_0\).
Then explain why we standardize \(\hat\theta\) to form a test statistic. We compute:

\[
z = \frac{\hat\theta - 0}{SE(\hat\theta)}
\]

Walk the reader through the logic of this standardization step by step:

By the CLT, we know that \(\hat\theta\) is approximately Normal for large samples. Under \(H_0\), the mean of that distribution is 0.
When we divide a Normal random variable by its standard deviation, we get a standard Normal \(N(0,1)\). So under \(H_0\), \(z \;\dot\sim\; N(0,1)\).
This means we know the distribution of our test statistic under the null, which is exactly what we need to compute a p-value.

Explain to the reader why this is sometimes called a “t-test” even though the test statistic follows an approximate Normal distribution, not a t-distribution. The classical t-test arises when the data are drawn from a Normal distribution and the variance must be estimated — the ratio then follows an exact t-distribution. In our setting the data are Bernoulli (not Normal), so there is no exact t-distribution result. The CLT gives us approximate Normality, and since we estimate the SE from the data, what we are really doing is closer to a z-test. In practice, for large samples the t-distribution and the standard Normal are nearly identical, so the distinction has little practical consequence — but it is important to understand why.
Using your simulated data, compute the test statistic and its associated p-value (using the standard Normal distribution as the reference). Interpret the result for the reader.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The T-Test as a Regression






Note




It turns out that the two-sample test we just ran is mathematically equivalent to a simple linear regression. Understanding this connection is useful because it means the same machinery — and the same software — that you use for regression can also perform hypothesis tests, and it generalizes naturally to more complex experimental designs.
Explain the setup to the reader. Stack the CTA A and CTA B data into a single dataset with two columns: an outcome \(Y_i\) (1 if the visitor signed up, 0 otherwise) and an indicator \(D_i\) (1 if the visitor saw CTA A, 0 if they saw CTA B). Then fit the regression:

\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \varepsilon_i
\]

Walk through the interpretation of the coefficients:

\(\beta_0\) is the expected value of \(Y_i\) when \(D_i = 0\) — i.e., the mean of the B group, which estimates \(\pi_B\).
\(\beta_0 + \beta_1\) is the expected value of \(Y_i\) when \(D_i = 1\) — i.e., the mean of the A group, which estimates \(\pi_A\).
Therefore \(\beta_1 = \pi_A - \pi_B = \theta\), and the OLS estimate \(\hat\beta_1\) is numerically identical to \(\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\).

Fit this regression using your simulated data. Report the coefficient estimate \(\hat\beta_1\), its standard error, its t-statistic, and its p-value. Compare these to the values you computed in the previous section using the two-sample approach — they should match (up to a small difference in how the standard error is computed; standard OLS assumes a single pooled variance, while the two-sample formula we used assumes separate variances for each group).
Explain to the reader why this equivalence matters: the regression framework makes it easy to add controls, interactions, or additional treatment arms, all while producing the same inference in the simple case.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Problem with Peeking






Note




Your boss is impatient. Rather than waiting until all 1,000 visitors have been assigned to each group, she wants to run the hypothesis test after every 100 visitors per group — peeking at the results after 100, 200, 300, …, up to 1,000 visitors per group (10 tests in total). If any of those tests comes back significant at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) level, she wants to declare a winner and stop the experiment early.
Explain to the reader why this is problematic under classical frequentist statistics. The key issue is that a single test at \(\alpha = 0.05\) has a 5% chance of a false positive (rejecting \(H_0\) when it is actually true). But when you conduct multiple tests on accumulating data, each peek is another opportunity to get a false positive. The overall probability of at least one false rejection across all the peeks is much higher than 5%.
Demonstrate this with a simulation. The idea is as follows:

Set up a world where the null hypothesis is true: \(\pi_A = \pi_B = 0.20\) (i.e., \(\theta = 0\), there is no difference between the CTAs).
Simulate a single experiment: draw 1,000 observations for group A and 1,000 for group B. After every 100 observations per group (at \(n = 100, 200, \ldots, 1000\)), compute the z-statistic and p-value. Record whether any of the 10 p-values falls below 0.05.
Repeat step 2 a total of 10,000 times to simulate 10,000 experiments.
Compute the fraction of those 10,000 experiments in which at least one peek produced a significant result. This is the empirical false positive rate under peeking.

Compare this to the nominal 5% false positive rate of a single test. Report the result and explain to the reader why peeking inflates the Type I error rate and what this means in practice for running A/B tests.
